question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y - 4)\ln (x - 1),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y - 4)\ln (x - 1)) \\  & =\frac{y - 4}{x - 1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y - 4)\ln (x - 1)) \\  & =\ln(x - 1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y - 4}{x - 1} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x - 1) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y - 4}{x - 1} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x - 1) \, \mathbf j = 0 \mathbf i + 0\mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y - 4}{x - 1}=0 \\ \ln(x - 1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y - 4=0,$ which means $y=4.$ From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x - 1)=0,$ which means that $x=2.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at the point $(2,4).$
